# Introduction

Every value in R has a **type**, and the type decides what you can do with it: you can add two read counts, but not a read count and a gene name. In this lab you will practise the lecture's topics using small examples from the lab bench. By the end you should be able to:

-   create values of the common data types and check their type,
-   convert between types on purpose (casting), and know that casting is not rounding,
-   recognise when R converts types for you (coercion), and why that can cause silent errors,
-   handle the special values `Inf`, `NaN` and `NA`,
-   use arithmetic, comparison and logical operators,
-   do basic text manipulation on gene names, sample IDs and DNA sequences.

## Data types

The four data types you will use every day:

| Type | What it holds | Lab example |
|:-----|:--------------|:------------|
| double | any number | Ct value `24.1`, temperature `37.5` |
| integer | whole numbers | read count `1523L` |
| character | text | gene `"BRCA1"`, sample `"S01"` |
| logical | `TRUE` or `FALSE` | treated? `TRUE` |

Numbers are stored as **doubles** by default, even whole numbers like `1523`. Add `L` to get an integer: `1523L`.

## Getting started

Open RStudio and open your `r-course` **Project** (File → Open Project…), so that R works in the right folder. You do not need `setwd()` when you use a Project.

List all objects in your current R session:

```{r}
ls()
```

If you want a clean start, the safest option is **Session → Restart R**. You can also remove all objects with:

```{r,eval=FALSE}
rm(list = ls())
```

<i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> This deletes everything in your environment. It uses functions we have not covered yet; it will make sense after the next lectures.

## Variables and data types

1. You are recording data for one mouse: its ID is **M07**, it weighs **23.4** g, it had **6** pups, and it is a **knockout** (`TRUE`). Store each value in a well-named variable and check its type with `typeof()`. Is the number of pups an integer? If not, make it one.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
mouse_id <- "M07"
weight_g <- 23.4
n_pups <- 6
knockout <- TRUE

typeof(mouse_id)
typeof(weight_g)
typeof(n_pups)    # "double": plain numbers are doubles
typeof(knockout)

n_pups <- 6L      # the L suffix makes an integer
typeof(n_pups)
```

A colleague stored the weight as `"23.4"` (in quotes). What happens if you add 1.5 g to it? How do you fix it?

```{r,accordion=TRUE,error=TRUE}
weight_text <- "23.4"
weight_text + 1.5               # error: you cannot do arithmetic on text
as.numeric(weight_text) + 1.5   # convert first
```

2. You have a DNA stock at **250** ng/µL and need **20** µL of a **10** ng/µL dilution. Using variables, calculate how many µL of stock and how many µL of water to mix. (Volume of stock = target concentration × final volume / stock concentration.)

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
stock_conc <- 250
target_conc <- 10
final_volume <- 20

stock_volume <- target_conc * final_volume / stock_conc
water_volume <- final_volume - stock_volume
stock_volume
water_volume
```

## Casting is not rounding

3. You have **250** samples and each plate holds **96**. How many plates do you need? Try `as.integer()`, `round()`, `floor()` and `ceiling()` on `250 / 96`. Which one gives the right answer here, and why are the others wrong?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
250 / 96
as.integer(250 / 96)   # 2: cuts off decimals, 58 samples have no plate!
round(250 / 96)        # 3, but only by luck: try 200 / 96
floor(250 / 96)        # 2: same problem as as.integer()
ceiling(250 / 96)      # 3: always rounds up, which is what we need
```

## Text, numbers and coercion

4. A plate reader exported these absorbance values. One well was too bright to measure (`"OVER"`) and one was left empty:

```{r}
absorbance <- c("0.84", "1.02", "OVER", "0.77", "")
```

What is the type of `absorbance`? Convert it to numbers and count how many values became `NA`. Then calculate the mean absorbance of the wells that were measured.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
typeof(absorbance)
abs_num <- as.numeric(absorbance)   # warning: NAs introduced by coercion
abs_num
sum(is.na(abs_num))                 # 2
mean(abs_num, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Write a sentence in your journal: `"OVER"` and `""` both became `NA`, but do they mean the same thing? Would dropping the `"OVER"` well bias your result?

5. Predict the type of each result, then check with `typeof()`:

```{r,eval=FALSE}
c(TRUE, 2L)
c("37", 5)
c(NA, 1L)
c(NA, "control")
```

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
typeof(c(TRUE, 2L))         # integer
typeof(c("37", 5))          # character: the number 5 becomes the text "5"
typeof(c(NA, 1L))           # integer: NA fits into any type
typeof(c(NA, "control"))    # character
```

## Special values

6. Three wells were imaged. Calculate the fraction of infected cells in each well, predicting the result first:

| Well | Infected cells | Total cells |
|:-----|---------------:|------------:|
| A1 | 12 | 40 |
| A2 | 0 | 35 |
| A3 | 0 | 0 |

Then calculate the log10 of these viral titres: 1,000,000, 1,000 and 0.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
12 / 40   # 0.3
0 / 35    # 0
0 / 0     # NaN: an empty well has no infection rate

log10(1e6)   # 6
log10(1e3)   # 3
log10(0)     # -Inf
```

7. Plant heights (cm) were measured, but two plants died before measurement:

```{r}
heights <- c(12.5, NA, 9.8, 15.1, 11.0, NA)
```

How many values are missing? What is the tallest plant? How many plants are taller than 10 cm? Why do you need `na.rm = TRUE` in all of them?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
sum(is.na(heights))
max(heights)                       # NA
max(heights, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(heights > 10)                  # NA: we don't know about the missing plants
sum(heights > 10, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Operators

8. In a population with allele frequencies `p = 0.65` and `q = 1 - p`, the Hardy–Weinberg genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q². Calculate them, then check that they add up to 1, first with `==` and then with `all.equal()`. What happened?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
p <- 0.65
q <- 1 - p
p^2
2 * p * q
q^2
p^2 + 2 * p * q + q^2 == 1                    # FALSE: rounding errors in decimals
isTRUE(all.equal(p^2 + 2 * p * q + q^2, 1))   # TRUE
```

9. You seed **100,000** cells that double every **20** hours. How many cells will you have after **72** hours? Use the formula cells = start × 2^(time / doubling time). Then use `sprintf()` or `round()` to report it as a whole number.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
start_cells <- 1e5
doubling_time <- 20
hours <- 72
cells <- start_cells * 2^(hours / doubling_time)
cells
round(cells)
```

10. A study includes patients who are **between 18 and 65 years old** (inclusive) **and** have **either** a BMI above 30 **or** diabetes. Write one expression that checks this for the patient below. Then change the values to test a few other patients. Why are the brackets important?

```{r}
age <- 52
bmi <- 27.4
diabetic <- TRUE
```

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
age >= 18 & age <= 65 & (bmi > 30 | diabetic)   # TRUE

# A 70-year-old diabetic patient should NOT be included:
age <- 70
age >= 18 & age <= 65 & (bmi > 30 | diabetic)   # FALSE: correct
age >= 18 & age <= 65 & bmi > 30 | diabetic     # TRUE: wrong! & is evaluated before |,
                                                # so every diabetic patient passes
```

11. These are the quality scores of eight sequencing reads. How many reads have a quality of at least 30? What **fraction** of the reads is that? Hint: what does `mean()` of `TRUE`/`FALSE` values give you?

```{r}
quality <- c(35, 28, 40, 31, 19, 38, 33, 25)
```

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
quality >= 30
sum(quality >= 30)    # 5 reads
mean(quality >= 30)   # 0.625: the fraction of TRUE values
```

12. Predict, then run. Explain each surprising result in your journal.

```{r,eval=FALSE}
sort(c("S1", "S2", "S10", "S11", "S3"))
"Control" == "control"
sqrt(2)^2 == 2
```

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
sort(c("S1", "S2", "S10", "S11", "S3"))   # "S10" and "S11" come before "S2"
"Control" == "control"                    # FALSE: comparisons are case-sensitive
sqrt(2)^2 == 2                            # FALSE: decimals are not stored exactly
isTRUE(all.equal(sqrt(2)^2, 2))           # TRUE
```

## Working with text

13. Here is a PCR primer:

```{r}
primer <- "ACGTTGCAGGCT"
```

- How long is it?
- Convert it to lower case (hint: `?toupper`).
- Does it start with `"ACG"`? (Extract the first three bases and compare.)
- Convert it to RNA by replacing every `T` with `U`. Try `sub()` first, then `gsub()`. What is the difference?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
nchar(primer)
tolower(primer)
substr(primer, start = 1, stop = 3) == "ACG"
sub("T", "U", primer)    # replaces only the first T
gsub("T", "U", primer)   # replaces every T
```

14. Build these names with `paste()`, `paste0()` and `sub()`:

- the well names of the first row of a 96-well plate: `"A1"`, `"A2"`, …, `"A12"`,
- the file names `"mouse_1.fastq"`, `"mouse_2.fastq"`, `"mouse_3.fastq"`,
- the sample name `"S3"` from the file name `"S3_R1.fastq.gz"`.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
paste0("A", 1:12)
paste0("mouse_", 1:3, ".fastq")
sub("_R1.fastq.gz", "", "S3_R1.fastq.gz")
```

15. Using `sprintf()` and your variables from exercise 2, print this pipetting instruction:

`Mix 0.80 uL stock with 19.20 uL water`

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
sprintf("Mix %.2f uL stock with %.2f uL water", stock_volume, water_volume)
```
